title: The Problem of Pain
subtitle: A Christian response to suffering
author: C. S. Lewis
description: A classic of Christian apologetics exploring why pain exists if God is good and all-powerful, and what answer faith offers.

1.
In this chapter I propose six propositions necessary to complete our
description of human suffering; these do not arise from each other and, therefore, must be
delivered in an arbitrary order.
1. In Christianity there is a paradox about the tribulation. Blessed are the
poor, but through "judgment" (i.e., social justice) and alms we must eliminate poverty
where possible. Blessed are we when they persecute us, but we can avoid the
persecution fleeing from city to city, and we can implore to be freed from it, so
as Our Lord implored in Gethsemane. But if suffering is good, shouldn't
be eagerly sought after, rather than avoided? My answer is that suffering is not
good in itself. The good thing about any painful experience is, for those who suffer, its abandonment
in the will of God, and for the spectators, the compassion it awakens and the acts of
mercy to those he leads. In the fallen and partially redeemed universe, we can
distinguish: 1) the simple good that descends from God, 2) the simple evil produced by
rebellious creatures, and 3) God's use of that evil for his redemptive purpose, and that
produces the complex good, to which the acceptance of suffering and the
repentance of sin. Now the fact that God can make an evil
simple, a complex good, does not excuse - even though through mercy it can
save—those who commit simple evil. And this distinction is fundamental. The offenses
they must come, but woe to those from whom they come; sins do make grace
abound, but we should not make it an excuse to continue sinning. The crucifixion is
the best and the worst of all historical events, but the role of Judas remains
simply evil. We can, first, apply this to the problem of the suffering of others.
people. A merciful man aspires to the good of his neighbor and thus fulfills "the will
of God", consciously cooperating with the "simple good". A cruel man oppresses his
neighbor and, thus, does simple evil. But in doing that evil he is used by God, without his
knowledge or consent, to produce the complex good - so that the first
of these men serves God as a son, and the second as an instrument.
You will certainly fulfill God's purpose no matter how you act, but for you it will be
It is different who serves as Judas, or as John. The entire system is, so to speak,
calculated for the clash between good men and bad men, and good
fruits of fortitude, patience, mercy and forgiveness, by which the cruel man is allowed
be cruel, they presuppose that the good man commonly continues to seek the simple good.
I say "commonly," because a man is sometimes authorized to hurt (or even, in my
opinion, to kill) his fellow man, but only when the need is urgent and the
good to obtain is obvious, and, generally (although not always), when he who inflicts
pain has a precise authority to do so—a fatherly authority, derived from the
nature; of magistrate or soldier, derived from civil society; or surgeon,
generally derived from the patient. Transform this into a general rule to afflict the
humanity, "because affliction is good for them" (as does Tamberlaine, the madman of
Marlowe, boasted of being the "scourge of God"), is certainly not breaking the scheme
divine, but to volunteer for the office of Satan, within that scheme. Yes
you do his job, you must be prepared to receive his pay.
The problem of avoiding our own suffering admits of a similar solution. Some
ascetics have used mortification. As a layman, I have no opinion on the wisdom of such
regime; but I insist that, whatever its merits, mortification is something quite
different from the tribulation sent by God. Everyone knows that fasting is an experience
different from skipping a meal by accident or due to poverty. Fasting affirms
will versus appetite, its reward being self-control, and its danger being pride; hunger
involuntarily submits the appetites and the will to the divine will, giving occasion to the
surrender and exposing ourselves to the danger of rebellion. But the redemptive effect of suffering
It lies, mainly, in its tendency to subdue the rebellious will. The practices
ascetic practices, which in themselves strengthen the will, are useful only to the extent that they make
possible for the will to order its own house (the passions), as a preparation for the
total offering of man to God. They are necessary as means; how they would end
abominable, since by substituting appetite for will and staying there, they would be
only changing the animal being for the diabolical being. Therefore, it has been truly said
that "only God can mortify." The tribulation fulfills its task, in a world where
Human beings commonly seek, through legitimate means, to avoid their own evil.
natural and achieve its natural good, and presupposes such a world. To submit the will to
God, we must possess a will, and that will must possess objects. The renunciation
Christian does not mean Stoic "apathy," but rather a willingness to choose God, rather than
do it for inferior purposes that are legitimate in themselves. Hence the Perfect Man led to
Gethsemane a will, and a strong will, to escape suffering and death,
provided this was compatible with the will of the Father, and combined with a
perfect disposition to obey, in case it were not. Some saints recommend a
"total renunciation" at the very beginning of our discipleship; but I think this can only
mean a total disposition to each specific renunciation 
60 that is required of us, since we do not
It would be possible to live minute by minute without wanting anything other than abandonment to God, as such.
What would be the matter for abandonment? It would seem contradictory in itself to say "what I want
is to submit what I desire to the will of God", since the second has no content. Without
No doubt, we all take great care to avoid our own pain: but an intention to
avoiding it, duly subordinated, and using legitimate methods, is in accordance with the
"nature"—that is, with the entire operating system of creature life,
for which the redemptive task of the tribulation is calculated.
It would be, therefore, quite false to assume that the Christian view of suffering is
incompatible with a strong emphasis on our obligation to leave the world, even in a
temporal sense, "better" than we found it. In the scene most full of parables
that He gave us, Our Lord seems to reduce all virtue to active beneficence; and to
Although it would be misleading to take that scene in isolation from the Gospel as a whole, it is
enough to dispel any doubt about the basic principles of the social ethics of the
Christianity.

60 Cf. BROTHER LAWRENCE., Prartice of the Presence of God. IVth conversation, November 25,
1667. A "single enthusiastic renunciation of everything to which we are sensitive does not lead us to
God."
2. If tribulation is a necessary element in redemption, we must expect it
will not cease until God sees that the world is already redeemed, or that it cannot be redeemed
more. Therefore, a Christian cannot believe any of those who promise that, if
only some reform would be carried out in our economic, political, or
health, we would have heaven on earth. This may seem to have an effect
discouraging in the social worker, but in practice it is not seen to discourage him. At
On the contrary, a strong sense of our common miseries, simply as men, is
at least as good an incentive to eliminate all the miseries we can, as
any of those crazy hopes that tempt men to seek to realize them
breaking the moral law and which, once carried out, prove to be only dust and ashes.
If we apply to our individual life the theory that an imagined heaven in the
earth, for there to be vigorous attempts to eliminate the present evil, would clearly demonstrate
immediate its irrationality. The hungry look for food and the sick for healing, even
knowing that after the meal or the cure, the normal ups and downs of life await them.
life. I am not, of course, arguing that very important changes are desirable or not.
drastic in our social system; I am only reminding the reader that a remedy
in particular it should not be confused with the elixir of life.
3. Since political issues have crossed our path, I must clarify that the doctrine
Christian abandonment and obedience is a purely theological doctrine and not, as far as
most minimal, politics. About forms of government, civil authority and civil obedience, nothing
I have to say. The type and degree of obedience that a creature owes to its Creator is unique,
because the relationship between creature and Creator is unique: no proposition can be inferred
her politics.
4. I believe that the Christian doctrine about suffering explains a very curious fact about
world we live in. The stable happiness and security we all desire is withheld
by God because of the very nature of the world; but He has poured out joy, pleasure and
joy, copiously. We are never safe, but we have many joys and some
ecstasy It's not hard to see why. The security we crave would teach us to put
our hearts in this world and would put an obstacle in our return to God. some
few moments of happy love, a landscape, a symphony, a happy meeting with our
friends, a bath, or a soccer game, have no such tendency. Our Father refreshes us
along the way with some pleasant inns, but we are not encouraged to confuse them with the
home.
5. We should never transform the problem of pain into something worse than it is, by
vague conversations about "the unimaginable sum of human misery." Suppose that
I have a toothache of intensity X, and suppose that you, who are sitting next to me,
He also begins to have a severe toothache. If you want, you can say that the
total amount of pain in the room is now 2X. But you must remember, that no one is
suffering 2X; Search all time and all space, and you will never find that pain
compound, in someone's conscience. There is no such thing as a sum of suffering,
since no one suffers from it. When we reach the maximum that a single person can suffer,
We have achieved, without a doubt, something very horrible, but we have achieved everything
suffering that can occur in the universe. Add a million people who suffer, no
adds more pain.
6. Of all evils, only pain is a sterilized and disinfected evil. the evil
intellectual, or error, can be repeated, because the cause of the first error (such as fatigue, or
bad handwriting) continues to operate; but, apart from that, error begets error because
own right—if the first step of an approach is wrong, everything that follows
will be wrong. Sin can be repeated, because the original temptation continues; but,
Apart from that, by its very nature, sin begets sin, through the
strengthening of sinful habit and weakening of conscience. Now, the
pain, like other evils, can of course be repeated, because the cause of the first
pain (an illness, or an enemy) is still operating; but the pain,
own right, it has no tendency to proliferate. Once it's over, it's over, and
natural consequence is joy. This distinction can be explained in reverse. After a
error, you not only need to eliminate the causes (fatigue or bad spelling), but also
also correct the error itself; after a sin he must not only, if possible,
eliminate temptation, you must also go back and repent of the sin itself. In each
case an "undo" is required. Pain requires no such undoing; you may need
cure the illness that caused it, but the pain is sterile once it is over, while
that every uncorrected mistake and every unrepentant sin are, by right
own, sources of new error and new sin, which flow until the end of time.
Once again, when I make a mistake, my mistake infects all those who believe in me.
When I sin publicly, each spectator either excuses it, thus sharing my guilt,
or condemns him, with imminent danger to his charity and humility. But the suffering is not
naturally produces bad effects on the spectators (unless they are
extraordinarily depraved), but a good effect: compassion. Therefore, that evil that
God uses mainly to produce the "complex good", it is manifestly
disinfected, or devoid of that tendency to proliferate, which is the worst characteristic
of evil in general.

Because of these, it is necessary to discuss the matter.
The problem is not simply a God who confines some of his creatures to ruin

the complexity of reality, presents us with something more tangled and more ambiguous—a God so
full of mercy, who becomes man and dies tortured to separate from his creatures

unable to prevent ruin by an act of mere power. A moment ago I said with

a thousandth of the price that God has already paid to eliminate the fact. And here is the
real problem: so much mercy, and yet there is hell.
I will not attempt to prove that the doctrine is tolerable. Make no mistake; It is not tolerable.
But I think it can be shown that the doctrine is moral, through a criticism of the

First, there is an objection in many minds to the idea of retributive punishment.
as such. This has been addressed, in part, in a previous chapter. There it was held that everything

sleeping like a healthy creature—a cheerful, rosy-cheeked man, without
care in the world, firmly confident, to the end, that he alone has

impregnable We must be cautious at this point. The slightest concession to the passion of
Revenge is a mortal sin. Christian charity advises us to make every effort
possible to convert that man: preferring his conversion—at the risk of our own
life, perhaps of our own soul—to its punishment; infinitely prefer it. But that's not him
matter. Assuming he does not want to be converted, what fate in the whole world
can you consider suitable for him? Can you really wish for such a man,
remaining what he is (and he must be able to do so if he has free will), were

all eternity, that he is the one who wins the game? And if you can't consider this
as tolerable, is it only his evil—only resentment—that prevents him from doing so? Or is it that
you find that the conflict between justice and mercy, which has sometimes
seemed such an outdated display of theology, are at this moment working in their
mind, and you feel as if it came from above, and not from below? You act not from a desire
of seeing the despicable creature suffer, but for a truly ethical demand of
that, sooner or later, good prevails, that the flag is implanted in this soul
horribly rebellious, even if there is no fuller and better conquest afterwards. In truth

And it seems to me that, although it makes us tremble, we agree. Demanding that God must
Forgiving such an individual, while he continues to be what he is, is based on a confusion

I have begun with the concept of hell as a positive, retributive, imposed punishment

62. We are then free—given

63. Our imaginary egoist has tried to turn everything

Another objection draws attention to the apparent disproportion between eternal damnation and

We think of time as a line—which is a good image, because the parts of time

Then, the entire reality of a human being would be represented by a solid figure. that

A third objection focuses attention on the terrifying intensity of the pains of hell,

Von Hügel here warns us not to confuse the doctrine itself with the images

Finally, it is objected that the final loss of a single soul means the defeat of the

Ultimately, the answer to all those who object to the doctrine of hell is itself
